item.title: Ten Players Who Didn’t Get a Hall of Fame Vote
item.description: And a few thoughts on the Cleveland forcing Game 5 in the ALDS.
item.dc:creator: Joe Posnanski
item.content:encoded:
Before we get to today’s big event — ten awesome baseball players who did not get a single Hall of Fame vote — we should talk for a minute about Chicago-Cleveland.

The Guardians beat the White Sox 9-5 to force a Game 5 in their American League Division Series. That game will be in Cleveland on Saturday at 8 p.m. Eastern. Neither team has announced their starter, but that’s OK because nobody cares who starts these playoff games anymore. The White Sox pulled their Game 4 starter, Hagen Smith, in the first inning. The Guardians pulled their starter, Parker Messick, in the third. There were fifteen pitchers in the game. Heck, the Guardians brought in Gavin Williams to finish off the game even though:

They had a four-run lead.

Williams was SUPPOSED to be the Game 5 starter.

He might still be the Game 5 starter. This series has been something else … six of the eight starters have been pulled after three or earlier. There are still a few stalwarts out there like the Miz or Yoshi*, but unless you’re one of the teams that can afford a pitcher like that (meaning: “The Dodgers”) or can develop one, every playoff game is a bullpen game.

*Speaking of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, I was talking with someone the other day who had just spoken at length with Atlanta’s legendary pitching coach, Leo Mazzone. My friend said he asked Mazzone what pitchers he admired in baseball today. Leo grimaced. “There are only two,” he grumped. “The Japanese guys. Yamamoto and Ohtani. They’re the only guys left who actually pitch. Everyone else is just throwing.”

But what stood out to me in Game 4 was, yes, José Ramírez. He’s going to be in the Baseball Hall of Fame someday; there’s no doubt in my mind about that, but this year has been rough. He’s been hurt. He’s slumped. He just hasn’t looked like himself at all. Is that surprising? Alas, it can’t be surprising — he’s 34 years old, and he’s 5-foot-9 and 190 pounds, and he plays 150-plus games pretty much every season. The clock ticks fast for players like that. You have to wonder:

Will he ever be THAT José Ramírez again?

We don’t know, can’t know, but I do know this: For the last two days, he has been that José Ramírez again. It isn’t just that he’s gone four-for-nine with a double, triple, home run, stolen base, four runs, and five RBI in those two games. No, he’s just looked spry, energized, as if the years have melted away. On Wednesday, he stole third base and scored on a hard ground ball to second because he got a fantastic jump. On Thursday, he smashed a home run on a 100-mph fastball at the top of the zone — the fastest pitch he’s ever hit for a homer, according to Sarah Langs — and later he came flying around third base to score on a single.

I think about which position players left in the tournament can, if they’re right, single-handedly carry their team to the title. Shohei would normally be at the top of the list, but he’s not right. Jackson Chourio is one, I think. Junior Caminero might be one. Freddie Freeman will have his clutch hits, and Mookie Betts does so many things. Munetaka Murakami has become must-watch TV. Kiké Hernández loves the postseason. Brice Turang is so good.

But if there were a draft, and I had to pick only one — I’d take the José Ramírez, who has looked like his old self.

I’m sending back my first-pass pages for FIFTY SEASONS on Monday, and the more times I re-read it, the more excited I am for it to come out on February 2. I really think you’ll love it. It’s filled with baseball stories and players that, I believe, will ignite your memory (“I remember that Andre Dawson season!”), and make you smile (Joe Wilhoit? Who? How?).*

*Of course, I have to say that preorders are now open everywhere — Barnes & Noble, Amazon, Bookshop.org, Target, our good friends at Rainy Day Books for signed copies, etc. — and that if you preorder now, you will get a special digital gift: The complete list of seasons and stories in the book, plus a bonus chapter about the invention of batting average. All you have to do is click here, scroll down, fill out the form, and you should get your gift automatically.

One thing: The form doesn’t work for international customers. But if you preorder the book internationally and send us your receipt, Kathleen and I will send you a link so you can get your gift.

FIFTY SEASONS is, nominally, a list book. I guess that’s my thing. I’ve always thought in lists, sometimes to my detriment. Years ago, when I was a columnist at The Kansas City Star, I used to write a weekly list column. And one day I was in the office, and my phone rang. It was Tom Watson. Yeah. The Tom Watson. We exchanged pleasantries, and then he said, “I want to ask you something. Do you want to be great?”

“I’m sorry?”

“Do you want to be a great columnist, like Jim Murray?”

“Um,” I said, “yes, of course I do.”

“Then,” Watson said triumphantly, “stop writing those damned list columns!”

But I do think in lists. It’s just a thing. I have a hundred lists sitting around the house — some on scraps of paper, some in notebooks, some on computer spreadsheets. I just can’t help myself.

This week’s list is 10 awesome players who received zero Hall of Fame votes. I’m only going back to 1979 because that was the year the Hall implemented the rule requiring players to get 5% of the vote to be included on the next year’s ballot. But I think 1979 is far back enough.

There are dozens of excellent players who never received a Hall of Fame vote — Reggie Sanders, Cecil Cooper, Dan Haren, Wally Joyner, Carl Crawford, Garry Maddox, Andy Van Slyke, Troy Glaus, Jose Rijo, on and on and on.

But here are the ten who, for different reasons, stand out in my mind.

item.title: The Brewers, the Padres and My Favorite Inning
item.description: Plus, I try on the Cincinnati Bengals as my next NFL team.
item.dc:creator: Joe Posnanski
item.content:encoded:
Let’s do a Wednesday free-for-all — we’re talking my favorite inning of the season, maybe the best story going in baseball, a suggestion for the Brewers … and some bonus football talk about why the Bengals just didn’t fit. All kinds of fun!

First, a couple of announcements. The good folks at Dutton are on Goodreads, and they’re giving away ten free galleys of my upcoming book, FIFTY SEASONS: Stories of the Baseball Years That Echo. Totally free to enter; all you have to do is head over to Goodreads and sign up.

There are 118 days left until FIFTY SEASONS comes out — the same as the number of triples credited to Hall of Famer Turkey Stearnes. You bet Turkey makes an appearance in the book; he’s one of my all-time favorites. Preorders are open everywhere. And if you preorder from our good friends at Rainy Day Books, I’ll sign the book and personalize it any way you like.

Molly Knight and I have had an incredible run of guests on The Joy of Baseball podcast … and I’d say, yeah, it continues this week as we talk with the one and only Nick Offerman. I call him the one and only Nick Offerman because, hey, I don’t know if you’ve seen these commercials during these playoffs, but it sure looks like Home Depot has hired some Nick-Offerman-light actor to talk about tools. I mean no offense to the actor himself — I’m all for actors finding work.

But, again, there’s only one Nick Offerman, and he’s the best, and he talks about the Cubs, about his love of the game, and about his baseball son, Payton Tolle.

Listen to it on your favorite podcast filling station.*

*We have been alerted that the podcast is not yet on Amazon Music … we’re working on it. If you have a favorite podcast platform and TJOB isn’t on it, let us know; we’ll see what we can do.

One other The Joy of Baseball tidbit — Molly Knight and I will be going live at 8 p.m. Eastern tonight to talk playoffs and whatever else comes to mind during the Yankees-Rays game. These live video chats are totally free, and we’d love for you to join. Our original idea was to make these subscriber exclusives — we were just looking to cover all the costs for The Joy of Baseball project, you know, producer costs, podcast costs, and all the extra time. But then Molly and I decided, no, the whole point of The Joy of Baseball is to bring, you know, the joy of baseball to folks.

Of course, we’d love for you to subscribe and be a bigger part of our community. It helps. But either way, we’d love to have you come along for the ride. An email will go out from here around 8 p.m. Eastern when Molly and I go live. Come on over. We have a great time.

Browns Diary: Trying on the Bengals

I will readily admit: I came into this week’s Bengals tryout with a lot of skepticism. Can I really become a Cincinnati Bengals fan after all these years of being a Browns fan? I mean, the Bengals were basically created by Paul Brown in defiance of the Browns — and in defiance of owner Art Modell, who had fired him.

PB chose the same colors. He built the team from the ground up, using all the lessons he had picked up over the Cleveland years. He took the most delicious delight in beating the Browns. The Cincinnati-Cleveland rivalry has been intense and sometimes nasty. Who can forget Bengals coach Sam Wyche chastising Bengals fans who were throwing snowballs on the field by shouting, “You don’t live in Cleveland!”

It seems to me that switching from the Browns to the Bengals is a bit like switching allegiances from Superman to Bizarro Superman. Can I really make that big a leap?

But I tried it for various reasons. One, I lived in Cincinnati for three years back in the 1990s, and I really love the city, and I had a lot of fun writing about some truly terrible Bengals teams. Two, my great pal Chardon Jimmy is a lifelong Bengals fan, and it would be a lot of fun to share the fan experience with him. Three, I like quarterback Joe Burrow a lot … I know the team I choose must have a quarterback I can fully get behind.

Four, it would be nice to have an excuse to order Skyline Chili three ways for Sundays.

I love Skyline Chili. I will not entertain dissent on this.

So I gave it a shot and, of course, things went very badly. It has not escaped my attention that the Browns have not lost since I walked out, nor that something very bad has happened to the Bears, Bills, and Bengals in the weeks I chose them. Bears quarterback Caleb Williams went down with a nasty non-contact hamstring injury. The Bills kept turning the ball over again and again like they had forgotten how to play football. And the Bengals lost their two superstar receivers in one game — Ja’Marr Chase suffered a concussion, and Tee Higgins went down with an abductor injury.

I have no idea what an abductor is. But it looked pretty awful.

I have a feeling that football fans everywhere will start offering me money to NOT root for their teams.

But there was actually a different reason why the Bengals didn’t quite take … even though Joe Burrow is a lot of fun to root for. I don’t think the Bengals know who they are. When you have a quarterback like Burrow and receivers like Chase and Higgins (when they’re healthy), it seems to me that you should be a high-flying, chance-taking, fast-and-loose kind of football team. But they’re not that. Coach Zac Taylor seems like a pretty buttoned-up guy, and his defense almost never blitzes, and the big offensive adjustment they made for 2026 is having Burrow line up behind the center more often.

Their personnel screams “Yahtzee!”

Their play style whispers “Risk.”

All game long, I was texting back and forth with Chardon Jimmy, and he felt pretty confident they would find a way to lose to the Jaguars — or at least find a way not to win — and sure enough, the game ended when, on fourth down and 10, with the Bengals just 21 yards away from the game-winning touchdown, Burrow threw short, and Chase Brown was tackled a yard short of the first-down marker.

“THAT is the most Bengal ending ever,” Jim wrote, and I believed him, and I thought: No, I don’t need to take on this pain. It feels too familiar.

Speaking of pain: Next week I’m going to try on the Detroit Lions.

This story is beyond belief …

Maybe you know the story of Atlanta’s Ray Kerr, who once dropped out of college and worked at a 7-Eleven. He has thrown six shutout innings in these playoffs. Wonderful.

But he might not even be the most wonderful story of the postseason.

Let me tell you about Tampa Bay’s Cam Booser.
